title: The Shopping List
tagline: Choose the rooms, then work out which ones are happiest as neighbours.
grownUp: A programme is the list of rooms a building needs. The Architect's wishes, from the chill-out room to the running track, are the start of the list.
Rooms have neighbours they like and neighbours they do not. Ask why a swimming pool wants a changing room close by, and why a library needs to be quiet.
The bubble diagram at home is an architect's first drawing. Keep it simple, and do not worry about neat lines.

steps.title: An architect's shopping list
steps.text: A programme is a list of all the rooms a school needs. The Architect's wishes are the start of the list.
steps.ask: Which wish would you put on the list first?

steps.title: Rooms like good neighbours
steps.text: Rooms have neighbours they like and neighbours they do not. A quiet library does not want a noisy hall right next door.
steps.ask: Which room would you put next to the library, and which room would you keep far away?

steps.title: Sort the room cards
steps.intro: Tap each room into noisy or quiet, then into wet or dry.

steps.title: Who wants to be next to the pool?
steps.prompt: Which room most wants to be next to the swimming pool?
steps.reveal: Swimmers need a changing room close by, so they do not have to walk far in wet swimming costumes. A government guide for school buildings says changing rooms should be near the sports areas.

steps.title: Make every face happy
steps.intro: Build a classroom, a hall and a library, then make sure every room's face is happy.

steps.title: Pool next door, or far away?
steps.scenario: Should the swimming pool sit right next to the chill-out room, or far away from it?

options.label: Right next to it
options.detail: Nobody has far to walk, so swimmers can get in and out quickly.

options.label: Far away
options.detail: The chill-out room stays calm and peaceful, because the pool is at the other end.

options.label: Close, with a corridor between
options.detail: The corridor catches some of the noise, and the walk is still short.

steps.reveal: Architects think about noise, wet feet and how far people walk. Some schools put the pool next to calm rooms, and others keep them well apart.
steps.followUp: If the pool was close to the chill-out room, what could you do to keep the noise out?

steps.title: Draw your house bubbles
steps: Draw one circle for each room in your house, and write its name inside it.
Put the circles for rooms that are next to each other close together, and the rooms that are far apart in different corners.
Join rooms with a line where people walk between them, and make the busiest lines thicker.
steps.why: A bubble diagram is an architect's first drawing. It shows which rooms should be neighbours before anyone draws any walls.

debrief: Which two rooms would you put next to each other at school, and why?
